executiveSummary: Chapter 19 explains how companies account for the differences that inevitably arise between pretax financial income (determined under IFRS) and taxable income (determined under tax law), requiring recognition of deferred tax assets and liabilities on the statement of financial position. Using the asset-liability method, the chapter demonstrates that income tax expense equals current taxes payable plus or minus the change in deferred tax balances, and addresses special topics including net operating loss carryforwards, uncertain tax positions, and the required IFRS disclosures and tax-rate reconciliation.
keyTopics: Pretax financial income vs. taxable income: IFRS-based book income and tax-authority taxable income frequently differ due to different recognition rules (e.g., accrual vs. modified-cash basis), creating temporary and permanent differences that drive deferred tax accounting.

Deferred tax liabilities arise from taxable temporary differences—situations where book income currently exceeds taxable income, meaning higher taxes will be owed in future periods (e.g., revenue recognised for book but deferred for tax).

Deferred tax assets arise from deductible temporary differences—situations where book expenses currently exceed tax deductions, meaning taxes will be lower in future periods (e.g., warranty accruals expensed for book but deductible only when paid).

Non-recognition (partial impairment) of deferred tax assets: A deferred tax asset must be reduced when it is probable (more than 50% likely) that some or all of it will not be realised; this reduction increases income tax expense in the current period.

Temporary vs. permanent differences: Temporary differences reverse over time and generate deferred taxes; permanent differences (e.g., non-deductible fines, tax-exempt bond interest) never reverse and therefore cause no deferred tax consequences, only affecting the effective tax rate.

Tax rate considerations: Deferred taxes must be measured using the enacted (or substantially enacted) future tax rate; when tax rates change, the full effect on existing deferred tax balances is recognised immediately as an adjustment to income tax expense.

Net operating loss (NOL) carryforwards: A company with a tax loss may carry it forward to reduce future taxable income; the expected future tax saving is recorded as a deferred tax asset, subject to the same probability assessment as other deferred tax assets.

Financial statement presentation and disclosure: Deferred tax assets and liabilities are classified as non-current; they may be offset when legally enforceable; IFRS requires disclosure of components of income tax expense and a numerical reconciliation between the statutory rate and the effective tax rate (intraperiod tax allocation).

importantDefinitions.Pretax financial income: Income before income taxes as computed under IFRS, also called income for book purposes; the basis for reporting to investors and creditors.
importantDefinitions.Taxable income: The excess of taxable revenues over tax-deductible expenses for a period as defined by the relevant tax authority; the base on which income taxes payable is calculated.
importantDefinitions.Temporary difference: The difference between the tax basis and the carrying (book) amount of an asset or liability that will result in taxable or deductible amounts in future years when the asset is recovered or the liability is settled.
importantDefinitions.Deferred tax liability: The deferred tax consequences attributable to taxable temporary differences; represents the increase in taxes payable in future years as a result of taxable temporary differences existing at the end of the current year.
importantDefinitions.Deferred tax asset: The deferred tax consequences attributable to deductible temporary differences and loss carryforwards; represents taxes that will be saved (refunded) in future years.
importantDefinitions.Permanent difference: A difference between pretax financial income and taxable income that arises from items recognised in one but never in the other (e.g., non-deductible fines, tax-exempt interest); creates no deferred tax balance.
importantDefinitions.Net operating loss (NOL): The excess of tax-deductible expenses over taxable revenues in a year; may be carried forward (and sometimes back) to offset income in other years, generating a deferred tax asset.
importantDefinitions.Loss carryforward: The provision allowing a company to apply the current year's net operating loss against taxable income in future years to reduce future taxes payable.
importantDefinitions.Effective tax rate: Total income tax expense for the period divided by pretax financial income; differs from the statutory rate when permanent differences or other adjustments exist.
importantDefinitions.Intraperiod tax allocation: The process of allocating total income tax expense among continuing operations, discontinued operations, other comprehensive income, and prior period adjustments within a single reporting period.
importantDefinitions.Substantially enacted tax rate: Under IFRS, the tax rate used to measure deferred taxes when a future rate change has been enacted or is virtually certain to be enacted; used instead of the current rate for periods when it applies.
importantDefinitions.Asset-liability method: The IASB-preferred approach to deferred tax accounting that focuses on reporting accurate deferred tax assets and liabilities on the statement of financial position, measured at the enacted rate expected to apply when the temporary difference reverses.

accountingTreatments: Recording a deferred tax liability (taxable temporary difference): Debit Income Tax Expense and credit Deferred Tax Liability for the increase in the cumulative temporary difference multiplied by the enacted future tax rate; simultaneously debit Income Tax Expense and credit Income Taxes Payable for current taxes owed. Example — Chelsea 2022: Dr Income Tax Expense $28,000 / Cr Income Taxes Payable $16,000 / Cr Deferred Tax Liability $12,000.

Recording a deferred tax asset (deductible temporary difference): Debit Deferred Tax Asset and credit the deferred portion of Income Tax Expense (a benefit) for the increase in the deferred tax asset; debit Income Tax Expense and credit Income Taxes Payable for current taxes. Example — Hunt 2022: Dr Income Tax Expense $180,000 / Dr Deferred Tax Asset $20,000 / Cr Income Taxes Payable $200,000.

Partial non-recognition of a deferred tax asset: When it is probable that a portion of a deferred tax asset will not be realised, debit Income Tax Expense and credit Deferred Tax Asset for the unrecoverable portion. If evidence improves, reverse with Dr Deferred Tax Asset / Cr Income Tax Expense.

Recording an NOL carryforward: In the loss year, if realisation is probable, debit Deferred Tax Asset and credit Income Tax Expense (Loss Carryforward) for NOL × enacted future tax rate. In the profitable year of realisation, debit Income Tax Expense and credit Deferred Tax Asset (to eliminate it) and Income Taxes Payable (for reduced taxes owed).

Tax rate change adjustment: When a new rate is enacted, remeasure all existing deferred tax balances at the new rate. Record the difference as Dr or Cr Deferred Tax Liability (or Asset) with the offset to Income Tax Expense in the period of enactment.

Loss carryback (Appendix 19B): In the loss year, debit Income Tax Refund Receivable (current asset) and credit Income Tax Expense (Loss Carryback) for the tax refund recoverable from prior years' taxes paid; any residual loss is treated as a carryforward deferred tax asset.
criticalFormulas: Income Tax Expense = Income Taxes Payable (or Refundable) +/- Change in Deferred Income Taxes. Variables: Income Taxes Payable = taxable income × enacted rate; Change in Deferred Income Taxes = ending deferred balance − beginning deferred balance (positive = expense; negative = benefit). Example: Payable $16,000 + Deferred increase $12,000 = Tax Expense $28,000 (Chelsea 2022).

Deferred Tax Liability = Cumulative Taxable Temporary Difference × Enacted Future Tax Rate. Variables: Cumulative difference = book basis of asset minus tax basis (or tax basis of liability minus book basis). Example: $30,000 receivable temporary difference × 40% = $12,000 DTL (Chelsea end of 2022).

Deferred Tax Asset = Cumulative Deductible Temporary Difference × Enacted Future Tax Rate. Variables: Cumulative difference = tax basis of liability minus book basis (or book basis of asset minus tax basis). Example: $50,000 litigation liability difference × 40% = $20,000 DTA (Hunt end of 2022).

Deferred Tax Expense (Benefit) = Ending Deferred Tax Liability − Beginning Deferred Tax Liability (for liabilities) OR Ending Deferred Tax Asset − Beginning Deferred Tax Asset (for assets, sign reversed for expense). Example: $12,000 DTL end − $0 DTL beginning = $12,000 deferred tax expense (Chelsea 2022).

Effective Tax Rate = Total Income Tax Expense / Pretax Financial Income. Variables: Total expense includes both current and deferred components; pretax income per IFRS books. Example: Bio-Tech 2021: $60,000 / $200,000 = 30%; 2022: $61,500 / $200,000 = 30.75% (due to permanent non-deductible insurance premium).
illustrativeExample: Akai Ltd. (Appendix 19A, 2021): Pretax financial income ¥412,000. Temporary differences: installment sales +¥448,000 taxable future amounts (DTL at 40% = ¥179,200); excess tax depreciation net ¥18,000 taxable (DTL = ¥7,200); warranty accruals ¥156,000 deductible (DTA at 40% = ¥62,400). Permanent differences: non-taxable bond interest −¥28,000; non-deductible fines +¥26,000. Taxable income = ¥100,000; income taxes payable (50% rate) = ¥50,000. Net deferred tax liability = ¥186,400 − ¥62,400 = ¥124,000 (non-current). Total income tax expense = ¥50,000 current + ¥124,000 deferred = ¥174,000. Journal entry: Dr Income Tax Expense ¥174,000 / Dr Deferred Tax Asset ¥62,400 / Cr Income Taxes Payable ¥50,000 / Cr Deferred Tax Liability ¥186,400. Net income = ¥412,000 − ¥174,000 = ¥238,000.
disclosurePresentationNotes: Statement of financial position: Current income taxes payable or receivable are classified as current liabilities or assets; all deferred tax assets and liabilities are classified as non-current and reported net (offset) when they relate to the same tax jurisdiction and there is a legally enforceable right of offset.

Income statement — intraperiod tax allocation: Income tax expense is allocated to continuing operations, discontinued operations, other comprehensive income, and prior period adjustments; both the current component and the deferred component must be disclosed either on the face of the income statement or in the notes.

Tax reconciliation disclosure (IAS 12): Companies must present a numerical reconciliation between reported income tax expense and the product of pretax accounting income multiplied by the applicable statutory tax rate, or alternatively a reconciliation between the average effective tax rate and the applicable statutory rate, explaining the reasons for any differences.

Loss carryforward disclosure: The amounts and expiration dates of operating loss carryforwards for tax purposes must be disclosed; this allows analysts to assess future periods in which the company will pay reduced or no income taxes and to evaluate the appropriateness of related deferred tax asset recognition.
potentialPitfalls: Confusing temporary and permanent differences: Permanent differences (e.g., non-deductible fines, tax-exempt interest) never create deferred tax assets or liabilities — they only affect the current year's effective tax rate. Erroneously recording a deferred tax balance for a permanent difference overstates assets or liabilities and distorts tax expense.

Using the wrong tax rate for deferred tax measurement: Deferred taxes must be measured at the enacted (or substantially enacted) rate expected to apply when the temporary difference reverses, not the current year's rate. When different rates apply to different future years, each reversal tranche must be multiplied by its applicable enacted rate (as illustrated by Wang Group). Using only the current rate when future rates differ will misstate deferred balances.

Incorrectly applying the probability threshold for deferred tax asset recognition: Under IFRS, a deferred tax asset (including for NOL carryforwards) is recognised only to the extent that realisation is 'probable' (more than 50% likely). Because this assessment is highly judgmental and relies on forecasts of future taxable income, companies may recognise an excessive asset during optimistic periods or fail to write it down quickly enough when negative evidence accumulates, creating earnings-management opportunities.

sources: Learning Objective 1 — Fundamentals of Accounting for Income Taxes (lines 100–636): covers pretax vs. taxable income, temporary differences, deferred tax liabilities (Chelsea Inc. example), deferred tax assets (Hunt Company example), and non-recognition of deferred tax assets.

Learning Objective 2 — Additional Issues (lines 637–935): covers income statement presentation formula, specific temporary and permanent differences (Bio-Tech AG example), tax rate considerations including future and revised rates (Wang Group and Hostel Co. examples).

Learning Objectives 3 and 4 — Loss Carryforwards and Financial Statement Presentation (lines 936–1413): covers NOL carryforward recognition and non-recognition (Groh Inc. example), uncertain tax positions, statement of financial position classification, intraperiod tax allocation, and tax reconciliation disclosures (Wm Morrison Supermarkets plc real-world example).
